title: What is an AI agent?
notes: An AI agent uses a language model to decide its own next steps, and takes actions with tools until it reaches a goal.
Every agent runs the same loop: perceive what is in front of it, decide the next step, act, then look at the result.
Autonomy is a dial, not a switch: give an agent the least power that does the job, and widen it as you trust it.

slides.title: What is an AI agent?
slides.sub: From a bot that can only talk to one that can look things up and act
sentences: Welcome to the course, and welcome to Orbit Outdoor.
Orbit is a small online shop for hiking, camping and climbing gear, and its support team is drowning in tickets.
Over six modules, you will build Scout, an AI agent that helps them.
In this first lesson, you will learn what an agent actually is, and what makes it different from a bot that only talks.

slides.title: Same question, two very different answers

left.label: Orbit's FAQ chatbot
points: Has no way to see orders
Replies: sorry, I can't check that

right.label: Scout, an agent
points: Decides to look up the order
Replies with the real tracking number

sentences: Start with the question Orbit hears all day long: where is my order?
Ana asks it in the website chat, and Orbit's current chatbot understands her perfectly.
But it has no way to see orders, so it apologises, and Ana is still waiting.
Now picture Scout, the agent you will build, getting the same question.
Scout decides it needs the order's status, looks it up, and reads the result.
Then it replies with the real status and the tracking number.
Both use the same kind of model underneath; the difference is that Scout can act.

slides.title: So, what is an AI agent?
slides.definition: A system that uses a language model to decide its own next steps, and takes actions with tools, until it reaches a goal.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A new colleague on the support team: you give them a goal and access to the order system, and they work out the clicks themselves.

sentences: Here is the definition we will use for the whole course.
An AI agent is built around a large language model, or LLM: a model that reads and writes text.
The model decides the next step itself, instead of following a script that someone wrote in advance.
It takes actions through tools, such as looking up an order or searching a policy document.
And it keeps going until it reaches a goal, like answering Ana with her real order status.
Think of a new colleague on the support team.
You give them a goal and access to the order system, and they work out the clicks themselves.

slides.title: The agent loop

note.text: Round again until the goal is met, or until a limit you set says stop.

sentences: Under the hood, every agent runs the same simple loop.
First, it perceives: it reads what is in front of it, like Ana's message.
Then it decides: given the goal, what is the most useful next step?
Then it acts: it calls a tool, such as the order lookup, or it writes the reply.
The result of that action is new information, so the loop starts again.
Scout perceives the order details, decides it now knows enough, and acts by replying.
The loop ends when the goal is met, or when a limit you set tells it to stop.

slides.title: One run, step by step

note.text: Two decisions, one tool call, one reply. Nobody wrote these steps in advance.

sentences: Here is one full run of that loop, step by step.
Ana's question arrives, with her order number in it.
Scout decides it can't answer from what it already knows, and that it needs the order status.
It calls the get order tool, and the result comes back: shipped with ParcelPath, tracking number included.
Scout looks at that result and decides it now has enough to answer.
It replies to Ana with the real status and the tracking number.
Two decisions, one tool call and one reply, and nobody wrote those steps in advance.

slides.title: How much should an agent do alone?
slides.lead: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. You choose where to set it.

bullets.text: Read only: look up orders and tracking, change nothing
Draft: write a reply that a person checks and sends
Act with approval: refunds over $200 wait for a person
Act alone: only small steps that are easy to undo

aside.label: Rule of thumb
aside.text: Give an agent the least power that does the job, and widen it as you learn to trust it.

sentences: Autonomy means how much an agent may do on its own, and it is a dial, not a switch.
At the low end, an agent only reads: it looks up orders and tracking, and changes nothing.
One step up, it drafts a reply, and a person checks it before it is sent.
Higher still, it takes real actions, but risky ones wait for approval, like Orbit's refunds over two hundred dollars.
Acting completely alone only makes sense for small steps that are easy to undo, because models can be wrong.
A good rule: give an agent the least power that does the job, and widen it as you learn to trust it.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: An agent uses a model to decide its own steps and acts with tools
It loops: perceive, decide, act, then look at the result
It stops when the goal is met or a limit says stop
Autonomy is a dial: start with the least power that does the job

sentences: Let's pull it together.
An agent uses a language model to decide its own steps, and acts through tools.
It runs a loop: perceive, decide, act, and then look at what happened.
It stops when the goal is met, or when a limit tells it to.
And autonomy is a dial, so start with the least power that does the job.
Next, we put agents side by side with chatbots and fixed workflows, and see when each one wins.

midQuiz.q: What can Scout do that Orbit's FAQ chatbot can't?
options: Understand what the customer is asking
Decide to use a tool, like an order lookup, and act on the result
Reply in a friendly, natural tone
midQuiz.explain: Both understand Ana's question and both write fluent text. Only Scout can act: it decides to call a tool, gets the real status and uses it.
midQuiz.hint: Both bots understood Ana perfectly. What could only one of them do next?

midQuiz.q: In the agent loop, what happens right after Scout calls a tool?
options: The run ends and the tool's raw output goes straight to the customer
Scout perceives the result and decides the next step
Scout starts again from Ana's first message and ignores the result
midQuiz.explain: A tool's result is new information. Scout reads it and decides again: another step, or the reply. That's why it's a loop.
midQuiz.hint: Perceive, decide, act... and then where does the loop go?

endQuiz.q: Which of these is an AI agent?
options: A bot that answers from a fixed list of FAQ answers
A script that emails every customer the same message at 8 AM
A system that reads a request, chooses which lookups to make, and replies with the results
endQuiz.explain: Only the third decides its own steps and acts with tools toward a goal. The first only talks; the second follows steps someone wrote in advance.
endQuiz.hint: Look for the one where the system, not a person, chooses what happens next.

endQuiz.q: Scout is getting a refund tool. What's the safest starting point?
options: Let Scout refund any amount on its own
Let Scout start refunds, but refunds over $200 wait for a person to approve
Never give Scout any tools at all
endQuiz.explain: Autonomy is a dial. Small, reversible steps can run alone; risky ones wait for a person. Orbit's policy already says refunds over $200 need approval.
endQuiz.hint: Think about the least power that still does the job, and what is hard to undo.
